criterion_notes.c1: Despite the title ('Who gets clean water?'), the study does not examine household or community access to drinking water or sanitation services. All units studied are existing community water systems (piping water daily to at least 15 connections or 25 year-round residents), and the study examines utilities' access to state infrastructure capital (loans and grants from PENNVEST) rather than water service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Borderline/yes as institutional background, because the study evaluates aid-allocation outcomes of a state financing agency (PENNVEST) and discusses its application process, one-year expiration policy, loan-repayment orientation, and U.S. EPA regulatory size classifications, although the sole empirically tested independent variable is water system population size rather than variation in a legal or administrative rule. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: No. Even where PENNVEST's application procedures, expiration rules, and screening practices are discussed interpretively, they govern utilities' acquisition of intergovernmental capital financing (construction loans and grants), not a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community water service access; moreover, administrative burden and screening rules are offered only as post-hoc explanations rather than measured exposures.
criterion_notes.c3: Quantitative empirical study analyzing linked state administrative records from the Pennsylvania Drinking Water Information System (2,331 community water systems) and PENNVEST construction funding applications (384 systems / 509 applications; analytic sample of 241 applications from 1988 to 1997) using Pearson chi-square and Mann-Whitney U tests.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports only whether community water systems applied to PENNVEST and whether completed construction applications received financial aid (loan/grant award vs. non-funding). No outcome measuring household or community water access, connection, service availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, disconnection/exclusion, or even SDWA water-quality compliance (which PA DEP declined to release) is reported.
criterion_notes.c5: Within the study's own public-finance scope, the unit of analysis and population (Pennsylvania community water systems and PENNVEST construction applications), exposure (system size measured by population served), outcome (application submission and PENNVEST funding receipt), and study design (cross-sectional quantitative analysis of administrative records) are clearly specified.

study_design: Quantitative observational cross-sectional analysis of linked state administrative databases (Pearson chi-square and Mann-Whitney U tests)
population_and_sample: Community water systems (CWS) in Pennsylvania: state inventory of 2,331 CWS (including 384 systems submitting 509 PENNVEST construction applications, 1988–1997) and an analytic sample of 241 PENNVEST construction project applications (191 funded, 50 not funded)
exposure: Water system size (population served by the community water system, analyzed via U.S. EPA three-class and five-class size categories and continuous population counts)
outcome: Application submission to PENNVEST (1988–1997) and receipt of PENNVEST infrastructure construction financial aid (loan and/or grant award vs. non-funding due to expiration, withdrawal, or rejection)
rationale: Excluded (E01 — Wrong topic; also fails c2/E03 and c4/E04). Although titled 'Who gets clean water?', this paper is an intergovernmental infrastructure-finance study examining whether small existing community water systems in Pennsylvania apply for and receive state construction loans and grants from PENNVEST ('access to capital'), not household or community water service access (c1=no). Empirically, the tested independent variable is utility population size rather than a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing water service access (c2=no under the 2026-10-13 clarification), and the reported outcomes are strictly grant/loan application and funding rates rather than water access, connection, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion (c4=no).
